An integer, N, is formed by writing the integers from 1 to 50 in order. That is,

N =1234567891011121314151617181920212223242526272829303132333435363738394041424344454647484950.

We will abbreviate N by writing only the first twelve positive integers and the last three integers, 48, 49, and 50. We place three dots between 12 and 48 to represent all of the integers between 12 and 48. So,

N = 123456789101112 . . . 484950

Some of the digits are selected from N and discarded. The remaining digits, in their original order, form a new integer such that the sum of the digits of this new number is 200.

topics.title: Excellent Math Problem from a Local Math Contest
topics.text:
Hello,

I just took a local math contest and one of the problems was the following:

[quote=Problem]Given an infinite amount of standard coins; $1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100$ cent coins, what is the smallest positive value of $n$ so that we cannot make $1$ dollar out of $n$ of these coins. [/quote]



My SolutionConsider for small cases:

$n=1$: $100$ cent coin.

$n=2$:  $50, 50$

$n=3$:  $50, 25, 25$

$n=4$:  $25, 25, 25, 25$

$n=5$:  $50, 25, 10, 10, 5$

$n=6$:  There are several ways to do this, one of them being $25, 25, 25, 10, 10, 5$.



Now note that for any $5, 25, 50$ cent coins we can split it into $5$ identical new coins. This creates $4$ more coins.

In particular, each $5$ or $50$ cent coin can add $4$ more coins; each $25$ cent coin can add $4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24$ more coins. Now we consider casework on the modulo of $n$ mod $4$:

[list]

[*] If $n \equiv 0 \mod 4$, then starting from the configuration for $n=4$, we can add any multiple of $4$ coins from $0$ to $96$. Thus all multiples of $4$ no greater than $100$ work.

[*] If $n \equiv 1 \mod 4$ then with the $n=5$ case we have that all $n \leqslant 37$ work.

[*] If $n \equiv 2 \mod 4$ then starting from the $n=6$ case we can get all numbers $\leqslant 82$.

[*] If $n \equiv 3 \mod 4$ then starting from $n=3$ we can get all numbers $\leqslant 55$.

[/list]



Thus we need to check $n=41$. However we see that $30$ pennies, $8$ nickels, and $3$ dimes work. As a result,

all $n \leqslant 73$ and congruent to $1 \mod 4$ work.

For $n=59$, consider $50$ pennies, $8$ nickels, and $1$ dime. Thus all numbers $\leqslant 91$ work.

It is not hard to check that $\boxed{77}$ does not work, which is our answer.

topics.title: Stars and Bars Clarification
topics.text:
Hi all,

I saw a problem that said:

' How many ways can you distribute 12 candies among four kids, if each kid gets at least one piece of candy?'

I then used to following logic:



' Ok, so there are 12 candies, among which there are 11 places for dividers (if each kid were to get one candy), and there can be 3 dividers (4 kids). Thus the solution is 11 C 3 = 165. '



I then checked the provided answer and saw that they derived the answer 455 using 15C3.

I don't understand what they did to get this answer, and I'm not sure why mine is not right. Could someone please explain what the flaw in my solution.



Thanks
